newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech trade deficit not expected to hit crown.
newsitem.headline: Czech trade deficit not expected to hit crown.

text.p: The Czech trade deficit posted another large rise in November but analysts said the figures were in line with their expectations and foresaw no negative effect on the rate of the Czech crown.

On Friday, the Czech statistical Office (CSU) said the November deficit was 16.6 billion crowns after 15.9 billion in October bringing the January to November figure to 140.1 billion crowns versus 81.4 billion in the same period in 1995.

"I think the results are not surprising, and they should not have a dramatic impact on the crown rate. Yesterday's very low GDP (gross domestic product) growth figures should have a larger impact than today's data," said Vladimir Kreidl, an economist at investment bank Patria Finance.
The CSU said on Thursday that third quarter GDP rose 3.6 percent year-on-year compared with 6.3 percent in the same period in 1995. Growth in the first three quarters of this year was 4.0 percent.
Boosted by Christmas sales, analysts said the trade gap would widen by a larger amount in December putting the full year 1996 deficit over 160 billion crowns.
But they said that the full year data should not have a big impact on the crown rate as investors had already discounted a deficit of such proportions into their expectations.

Kreidl said the most worrying aspect of Friday's trade figures was the downturn in exports. Exports actually fell, by 3.8 percent in nominal terms, in November and grew by just 4.4 percent in the January to November period.
Imports, meanwhile rose a nominal 13.4 percent in the first 11 months and 7.9 percent in November. November year-on-year inflation stood at 8.6 percent.
Despite Kreidl's reservations, however, some analysts drew comfort from the fall in the rate of import growth in November.
"I would not overestimate the fall in exports, because there was also a slowdown in the dynamics of imports as well," said Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka.

Immediately after the trade figures were release, the Czech crown dipped slightly but recovered almost immediately. Since early morning the crown has sustained levels of around 27.4 crowns to the dollar and 17.5 crowns to the mark.
Central bank and government officials have repeatedly ruled out devaluation as a way to improve the trade balance.
Officials and analysts say the balloning Czech trade deficit has been exacerbated by the recession in western Europe, expecially in Germany.
Kreidl said he expected that the widely predicted upturn in Germany, which is the country's largest trade partner, would lead to an increase of export pace next year.

The CSU predicts a 163.3 billion crown trade deficit for the whole year, putting the current account deficit up to 6.9 percent of GDP. It said the trade deficit would reach 200 to 210 billion crowns next year.
